display_title: [XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

Previously, `--xla_gpu_execution_progress_tracking` only wired its progress dump to the host-side terminate watchdog (`--xla_gpu_execution_terminate_timeout`). When a kernel or collective hung on the device after host dispatch returned (`--xla_gpu_device_execution_terminate_timeout` or `ExecutionTimeoutHandler`), the process aborted without logging completed or pending thunks.

So this change extracts `LogExecutionProgress` (logging `[<device_ordinal>]` context on every line, nested `kCommandBuffer` thunks for pending command buffers, and `Last pending thunks` only when `num_pending > max_thunks_to_log`) and wires it to `HangWatchdog::Abort` for both host and device terminate timeouts as well as `ExecutionTimeoutGuards` via `std::shared_ptr<ProgressTracker>` captured in the watchdog callbacks (which `device_guards` keeps alive in `main_stream->DoHostCallback` until enqueued device work completes).

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1024534356

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Use typed steps in ShapeTracker and add a generic Append.

`ShapeTracker::Step` is now a `std::variant<Reshape, Transpose, Broadcast,
Reduce>` of typed structs instead of one struct whose fields meant different
things depending on its type. `Append(const Step&)` applies any step.

The `Prepend*` methods now share one private implementation that inverts the
tracker, appends the inverse of the step and inverts back. Invalid `Prepend*`
calls now fail without changing the tracker; otherwise there is no behavior
change.

This prepares for slice and pad steps.

PR #52609: [ROCm] Port StreamExecutor test cases and fix the gaps they expose

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52609

📝 Summary of Changes
- RocmExecutor::IsHostMemoryPinned left start_addr/range_size
  uninitialized when hipDrvPointerGetAttributes does not populate them,
  so the containment check read indeterminate stack values.

- RocmExecutor::GetPointerMemorySpace returned InternalError for

  first and maps managed/unified memory types to MemorySpace::kUnified

- RocmStream only declared the single-argument DoHostCallbackWithStatus,
  which name-hid the error_cb overload and silently dropped asynchronous
  callback failures. The overload is now implemented, including invoking
  error_cb when the callback cannot be enqueued.

Test cases added:
  - rocm_kernel_test:   ArityZeroKernelSkipsArgumentCountCheck
  - rocm_executor_test: IsHostMemoryPinnedWorksWithRegisteredHostMemory
                      GetPointerMemorySpaceWorksWithUnifiedMemory
  - rocm_stream_test:   DoHostCallbackWithStatusSuccess
                      DoHostCallbackWithStatusError

🎯 Justification
Add more unit test coverage on ROCm platform

display_title: PR #50727: [CPU] Flush subnormal inputs in the atan2 builtins

head_commit.message:
PR #50727: [CPU] Flush subnormal inputs in the atan2 builtins

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50727

## Summary

XLA:CPU executes libm calls with flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero enabled, and glibc's `atan2`/`atan2f` misbehave on subnormal inputs in that state: subnormal pairs can give the wrong quadrant (for example `atan2(2^-1074, 2^-1074)` returns pi/2 instead of the correct result for flushed inputs), and `atan2f(denorm_min, 1)` can return NaN.

This registers guarded `BuiltinAtan2` and `BuiltinAtan2f` CPU builtins that flush subnormal inputs to signed zero before calling libm. A single templated helper inspects the operand bits (floating-point comparisons can already treat subnormals as zero under DAZ), flushes only nonzero subnormals, and preserves each flushed input's sign so quadrant selection still works. Signed zeros, infinities, and NaNs pass through unchanged. The builtins do not read or modify the floating-point environment, so no denormal state is saved, changed, or restored around the libm call.

Fixes tensorflow/tensorflow#129083.

## Kind of contribution

Bug fix and regression tests.

## Tests and validation

- `//xla/backends/cpu/codegen:builtin_atan2_test`:
  - Hardcoded expectations for flushed f64 and f32 subnormal inputs. Once the inputs are zeroed, every case reduces to one of +/-0, +/-pi/2, or +/-pi.
  - A cross-product loop over subnormal, normal, signed-zero, infinity, and NaN operands under all four FTZ/DAZ state combinations checks that the caller's denormal state is left untouched and that non-subnormal inputs pass through unchanged (compared against `std::atan2`/`atan2f` called directly).
  - `GlibcDenormalMisbehaviors` covers the specific wrong-quadrant and NaN cases seen with glibc.
- `//xla/tests:atan2_test`: new `F64SubnormalOperands` and `F32SubnormalOperands` cases with hardcoded expected results. They use runtime parameters so the subnormal inputs reach compiled code instead of being constant-folded, and they are guarded to CPU only (`test::DeviceTypeIs(test::kCpu)`) because GPU does not zero subnormals and returns pi/4 for `atan2(tiny, tiny)`.
- The issue was reproduced on Linux x86-64 emulation with the reported `tf-nightly==2.23.0.dev20261011`, with the original input bits preserved, and confirmed in a direct libm probe with FTZ/DAZ enabled.
- In this update, `builtin_atan2.cc` was also compiled and run standalone to check the templated helper (flushed pair gives +0, opposite signs give pi, a normal operand against a flushed one gives pi/2, and the f32 case is not NaN). A full local Bazel run of the updated tests was not possible in the current environment (the local Bazel server cannot start), so those results are pending CI.

## Performance

The normal-input path only adds bit inspection of the two operands before the libm call; there is no floating-point state change to pay for. No benchmark numbers are claimed for this version.

[XLA:GPU] Test all supported elementwise ops in `fusion_emitter_parametrized_test`.

`UnaryElementwiseTest` and `BinaryElementwiseTest` check the numerical results
of elementwise ops emitted by the generic Triton emitter, but only covered a
fixed list of opcodes and types inherited from the legacy Triton support
helpers.

They now test the same opcodes as `support_test.cc` (except ops whose result
type differs from their operand type, and comparisons, which have their own
test) across a broad set of types, and skip a case if
`IsTritonSupportedComputation` reports the test fusion as unsupported on the
current device. This makes them check that everything the support check allows also
produces correct results. `DoesOpSupportType` moves from `support_test.cc` to
`test_utils` so both tests can use it.

This is part of the effort to remove `support_legacy.cc`.

display_title: Use stable_sort in Triton AllocateWarpGroups and re-enable lit test.

head_commit.message:
Use stable_sort in Triton AllocateWarpGroups and re-enable lit test.

`AllocateWarpGroups` sorted warp-group partitions by descending warp count with unstable `llvm::sort`. When two partitions have equal warp counts, standard library implementations such as libc++ can reorder them. That reordering changes `warpGroupStartIds` and breaks `test/Conversion/allocate_warp_groups.mlir`.

Switch to `llvm::stable_sort` so equal-sized partitions keep their original relative order, and re-enable `Conversion/allocate_warp_groups.mlir`.

display_title: [JAX] Use the new XLA autotuner cache flags for the persistent compilation cache.

head_commit.message:
[JAX] Use the new XLA autotuner cache flags for the persistent compilation cache.

XLA deprecated `xla_gpu_per_fusion_autotune_cache_dir` and `xla_gpu_experimental_autotune_cache_mode` in favor of backend-neutral `xla_autotune_cache_dir` and `xla_autotune_cache_mode`.

Expose the new autotune cache `DebugOptions` fields in jaxlib and bump `jaxlib_extension_version` to 526. When jaxlib is new enough, JAX's persistent compilation cache now sets the new fields, and the cache key ignores them (both in `DebugOptions` and in `XLA_FLAGS`) the same way it already ignores the deprecated ones, so users switching to the new flags don't get cache misses. Older jaxlib versions keep using the deprecated fields.

The on-disk subdirectory name and the `jax_persistent_cache_enable_xla_caches` option values are unchanged, so existing caches and configurations keep working.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1012576594

display_title: Use stable_sort in Triton AllocateWarpGroups and re-enable lit test.

head_commit.message:
Use stable_sort in Triton AllocateWarpGroups and re-enable lit test.

`AllocateWarpGroups` sorted warp-group partitions by descending warp count with unstable `llvm::sort`. When two partitions have equal warp counts, standard library implementations such as libc++ can reorder them. That reordering changes `warpGroupStartIds` and breaks `test/Conversion/allocate_warp_groups.mlir`.

Switch to `llvm::stable_sort` so equal-sized partitions keep their original relative order, and re-enable `Conversion/allocate_warp_groups.mlir`.

head_commit.message:
PR #52821: [XLA:GPU] Run stream-annotated computations on locality domains

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52821

📝 Summary of Changes

Lets an XLA program run a computation on a chosen locality domain by annotating a call with `_xla_stream_annotation="locality_domain:<id>"`. Builds on the stream building blocks ([#52124](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52124)) and their execution support ([#52246](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52302)).
- `ExplicitStreamAnnotationAsyncWrapper`: wraps a locality-domain-annotated call into an async region. It rejects regions that contain collectives, send/recv or nested stream annotations, and annotations that aren't on a non-inlineable call.
- `ExecutionStreamAssignment`: assigns `LocalityDomainStreamId(<id>)` to those regions, without using up a round-robin compute stream.
- `AsyncStartThunk::Prepare`: rejects communication thunks inside a locality-domain region at runtime.
- **MHLO → HLO**: stream annotations stay on the call, not on the get-tuple-elements that unpack a multi-result call.
- `side_effect_util`: adds `kXlaLocalityDomainStreamAnnotationPrefix` (`"locality_domain:"`).

🎯 Justification

This is the first PR that lets a program annotate calls to run on a locality domain's stream, using the runtime support from [#52246](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52302). Programs without these annotations are unchanged.

🚀 Kind of Contribution

✨ New Feature, 🧪 Tests

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

N/A: this enables locality-domain execution

🧪 Unit Tests:

- `ExecutionStreamAssignmentTest`:
  - `ValidLocalityDomainAnnotationTest.AssignsLocalityDomainStream`;
  - `MalformedLocalityDomainAnnotationTest.DiesWithCheckMessage`;
  - `LocalityDomainAnnotationRejectsCommunicationScope`;
  - `LocalityDomainDoesNotConsumeRoundRobinStream`.
- `ExplicitStreamAnnotationAsyncWrapperTest` (10 tests):
  - wrapping a call while keeping its attributes; idempotence; tuple calls with get-tuple-element users;
  - rejecting missing or inlineable calls, transitive collectives, nested annotations and send/recv;
  - returning an error status inside fusions and async computations.
- `AsyncThunkTest.LocalityDomainPrepareRejectsCommunicationThunks`: a compute-only region prepares successfully, and one containing a communication thunk is rejected.
- `frontend_attributes.mlir`: stream annotations aren't copied onto the get-tuple-elements of a multi-result call.

🧪 Execution Tests:

`LocalityDomainComputeTest` runs on a single GPU, and skips on GPUs with fewer than two locality domains.
- `AnnotatedCallsBecomeLocalityDomainRegions`: two dependent calls annotated `locality_domain:0` and `locality_domain:1` become async regions on their domains in the optimized module.
- `AnnotatedCallsProduceCorrectResults`: the same program matches the interpreter's results.

wrapped into an async region by ExplicitStreamAnnotationAsyncWrapper and
assigned LocalityDomainStreamId(<id>) by ExecutionStreamAssignment, so it
runs on that domain's stream. The wrapper rejects locality-domain regions
that contain collectives, send/recv or nested stream annotations, and
AsyncStartThunk::Prepare rejects communication thunks inside them at
runtime. Stream annotations are kept only on the call, not on the
get-tuple-elements that unpack a multi-result call.

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

Previously, `--xla_gpu_execution_progress_tracking` only wired its progress dump to the host-side terminate watchdog (`--xla_gpu_execution_terminate_timeout`). When a kernel or collective hung on the device after host dispatch returned (`--xla_gpu_device_execution_terminate_timeout` or `ExecutionTimeoutHandler`), the process aborted without logging completed or pending thunks.

So this change extracts `LogExecutionProgress` (logging `[<device_ordinal>]` context on every line, nested `kCommandBuffer` thunks for pending command buffers, and `Last pending thunks` only when `num_pending > max_thunks_to_log`) and wires it to `HangWatchdog::Abort` for both host and device terminate timeouts as well as `ExecutionTimeoutGuards` via `std::shared_ptr<ProgressTracker>` captured in the watchdog callbacks (which `device_guards` keeps alive in `main_stream->DoHostCallback` until enqueued device work completes).

display_title: [XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

Region live range analysis repeatedly queried
`HloOrdering::GetExecutionConstraint` and linearly scanned accumulated control
edges on unordered instruction pairs, causing cubic blowups on high fanout
operands inside conditional branches. It also copied per computation instruction
maps on membership checks and scanned all region pairs after interference was
decided.

Answer same computation ordering queries directly from `HloReachabilityMap`
combined with transitive ancestor bitvectors over tentative control edges, and
cache directed cross computation queries. Store `LiveRangeRegions` as sorted
flat vectors, test smaller computation pairs first, stop scanning once
interference is forced, and add a same computation fast path in
`CallGraph::NearestAncestorsInSameComputation`. Move region analysis internals
into `copy_removal.cc`, replace `Relation` with a three bit ordering mask,
replace the per copy analysis budget in `CopyRemover::TryElideCopy` with
`ElideOptions`, store value nodes in a deque, and unify head and tail merge
checks.

Tests:
- `//xla/service:copy_insertion_test`: covers copy elision with many unordered
  readers, high fanout constant conditionals, transitive control edge cycle
  prevention, and interfering reads.
PiperOrigin-RevId: 1024508205

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Replace reduction tile pruning with strided opt-in selection

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Replace reduction tile pruning with strided opt-in selection

Pruning was wasteful as a strategy as it still hits the compile-time due to trying many configurations that aren't useful. Instead, the microbenchmarks were analyzed to see where we improve with tiling reduction dimensions. This change uses an opt-in strategy instead.

The most impactful cases were shown to be column reductions. For these cases tiling the reduce dimension allows us to use bigger tiles for minor parallel dimensions that can benefit from coalescing. The thresholds used are empirical from the data, but they look reasonable.

The change only applies behind flags, so production is unaffected. Follow-up changes will modify the cost model to improve the top-1 candidates and enable tiled reductions for kernels with no more than one reduce op.

display_title: PR #50727: [CPU] Flush subnormal inputs in the atan2 builtins

head_commit.message:
PR #50727: [CPU] Flush subnormal inputs in the atan2 builtins

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50727

## Summary

XLA:CPU executes libm calls with flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero enabled, and glibc's `atan2`/`atan2f` misbehave on subnormal inputs in that state: subnormal pairs can give the wrong quadrant (for example `atan2(2^-1074, 2^-1074)` returns pi/2 instead of the correct result for flushed inputs), and `atan2f(denorm_min, 1)` can return NaN.

This registers guarded `BuiltinAtan2` and `BuiltinAtan2f` CPU builtins that flush subnormal inputs to signed zero before calling libm. A single templated helper inspects the operand bits (floating-point comparisons can already treat subnormals as zero under DAZ), flushes only nonzero subnormals, and preserves each flushed input's sign so quadrant selection still works. Signed zeros, infinities, and NaNs pass through unchanged. The builtins do not read or modify the floating-point environment, so no denormal state is saved, changed, or restored around the libm call.

Fixes tensorflow/tensorflow#129083.

## Kind of contribution

Bug fix and regression tests.

## Tests and validation

- `//xla/backends/cpu/codegen:builtin_atan2_test`:
  - Hardcoded expectations for flushed f64 and f32 subnormal inputs. Once the inputs are zeroed, every case reduces to one of +/-0, +/-pi/2, or +/-pi.

display_title: Use stable_sort in Triton AllocateWarpGroups and re-enable lit test.

head_commit.message:
Use stable_sort in Triton AllocateWarpGroups and re-enable lit test.

`AllocateWarpGroups` sorted warp-group partitions by descending warp count with unstable `llvm::sort`. When two partitions have equal warp counts, standard library implementations such as libc++ can reorder them. That reordering changes `warpGroupStartIds` and breaks `test/Conversion/allocate_warp_groups.mlir`.

Switch to `llvm::stable_sort` so equal-sized partitions keep their original relative order, and re-enable `Conversion/allocate_warp_groups.mlir`.

head_commit.message:
PR #50727: [CPU] Flush subnormal inputs in the atan2 builtins

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/50727

## Summary

XLA:CPU executes libm calls with flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero enabled, and glibc's `atan2`/`atan2f` misbehave on subnormal inputs in that state: subnormal pairs can give the wrong quadrant (for example `atan2(2^-1074, 2^-1074)` returns pi/2 instead of the correct result for flushed inputs), and `atan2f(denorm_min, 1)` can return NaN.

This registers guarded `BuiltinAtan2` and `BuiltinAtan2f` CPU builtins that flush subnormal inputs to signed zero before calling libm. A single templated helper inspects the operand bits (floating-point comparisons can already treat subnormals as zero under DAZ), flushes only nonzero subnormals, and preserves each flushed input's sign so quadrant selection still works. Signed zeros, infinities, and NaNs pass through unchanged. The builtins do not read or modify the floating-point environment, so no denormal state is saved, changed, or restored around the libm call.

Fixes tensorflow/tensorflow#129083.

## Kind of contribution

Bug fix and regression tests.

## Tests and validation

- `//xla/backends/cpu/codegen:builtin_atan2_test`:
  - Hardcoded expectations for flushed f64 and f32 subnormal inputs. Once the inputs are zeroed, every case reduces to one of +/-0, +/-pi/2, or +/-pi.
  - A cross-product loop over subnormal, normal, signed-zero, infinity, and NaN operands under all four FTZ/DAZ state combinations checks that the caller's denormal state is left untouched and that non-subnormal inputs pass through unchanged (compared against `std::atan2`/`atan2f` called directly).
  - `GlibcDenormalMisbehaviors` covers the specific wrong-quadrant and NaN cases seen with glibc.
- `//xla/tests:atan2_test`: new `F64SubnormalOperands` and `F32SubnormalOperands` cases with hardcoded expected results. They use runtime parameters so the subnormal inputs reach compiled code instead of being constant-folded, and they are guarded to CPU only (`test::DeviceTypeIs(test::kCpu)`) because GPU does not zero subnormals and returns pi/4 for `atan2(tiny, tiny)`.
- The issue was reproduced on Linux x86-64 emulation with the reported `tf-nightly==2.23.0.dev20261011`, with the original input bits preserved, and confirmed in a direct libm probe with FTZ/DAZ enabled.
- In this update, `builtin_atan2.cc` was also compiled and run standalone to check the templated helper (flushed pair gives +0, opposite signs give pi, a normal operand against a flushed one gives pi/2, and the f32 case is not NaN). A full local Bazel run of the updated tests was not possible in the current environment (the local Bazel server cannot start), so those results are pending CI.

## Performance

The normal-input path only adds bit inspection of the two operands before the libm call; there is no floating-point state change to pay for. No benchmark numbers are claimed for this version.

name: CI ROCm
display_title: [XLA:GPU] Add CuDnnGemmDimensions to compute the dimensions of cuDNN GEMM fusions with ShapeTracker.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Add CuDnnGemmDimensions to compute the dimensions of cuDNN GEMM fusions with ShapeTracker.

`CuDnnFusionCompiler` derives the sizes and strides of the tensors of dot /
scaled-dot cuDNN fusions with `TritonFusionAnalysis`, which is part of the
legacy Triton GEMM tiling infrastructure that we want to remove: it no longer
tiles or emits fusions and does not support many of today's fusions.

`CuDnnGemmDimensions` replaces it in a follow-up change (cl/1018233906), using these steps:

1.  Use ShapeTracker to relate every instruction to one 'port' of the dot (lhs, rhs, output).
2.  Check cuDNN restrictions (i.e. non-scalar instructions must relate to the dot in a single way, because the cuDNN graph has a single tensor per instruction - for example, `dot(p, p)` and `d + transpose(d)` are rejected).
3.  Use ShapeTracker to record sizes and strides of each operand and output. This translates all bitcasts/transposes that are allowed into sizes and strides for cuDNN to read the correct tensor for operand (e.g. [batch, M, K] for lhs).

I haven't replaced TritonFusionAnalysis immediately because I still need to support strides and split-M, which happen in follow up CLs.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1024496195

name: CI ROCm
display_title: [XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

Region live range analysis repeatedly queried
`HloOrdering::GetExecutionConstraint` and linearly scanned accumulated control
edges on unordered instruction pairs, causing cubic blowups on high fanout
operands inside conditional branches. It also copied per computation instruction
maps on membership checks and scanned all region pairs after interference was
decided.

Answer same computation ordering queries directly from `HloReachabilityMap`
combined with transitive ancestor bitvectors over tentative control edges, and
cache directed cross computation queries. Store `LiveRangeRegions` as sorted
flat vectors, test smaller computation pairs first, stop scanning once
interference is forced, and add a same computation fast path in
`CallGraph::NearestAncestorsInSameComputation`. Move region analysis internals
into `copy_removal.cc`, replace `Relation` with a three bit ordering mask,
replace the per copy analysis budget in `CopyRemover::TryElideCopy` with
`ElideOptions`, store value nodes in a deque, and unify head and tail merge
checks.

Tests:
- `//xla/service:copy_insertion_test`: covers copy elision with many unordered
  readers, high fanout constant conditionals, transitive control edge cycle
  prevention, and interfering reads.

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

Previously, `--xla_gpu_execution_progress_tracking` only wired its progress dump to the host-side terminate watchdog (`--xla_gpu_execution_terminate_timeout`). When a kernel or collective hung on the device after host dispatch returned (`--xla_gpu_device_execution_terminate_timeout` or `ExecutionTimeoutHandler`), the process aborted without logging completed or pending thunks.

So this change extracts `LogExecutionProgress` (logging `[<device_ordinal>]` context on every line, nested `kCommandBuffer` thunks for pending command buffers, and `Last pending thunks` only when `num_pending > max_thunks_to_log`) and wires it to `HangWatchdog::Abort` for both host and device terminate timeouts as well as `ExecutionTimeoutGuards` via `std::shared_ptr<ProgressTracker>` captured in the watchdog callbacks (which `device_guards` keeps alive in `main_stream->DoHostCallback` until enqueued device work completes).

name: CI ROCm
display_title: Fix spatial-minor backward weight conv rewrite on v6e+

head_commit.message:
Fix spatial-minor backward weight conv rewrite on v6e+

Small-batch and small-input-feature 2D backward-weight (`window_dilation`)
convolutions waste most of each 2D tile under spatial-major layouts and require
expensive layout-conversion copies, whereas spatial-minor lowering places a
large spatial dimension in the minor tile dimension directly. Right now,
`SpaceToBatchConverter` propagates splits into these convolutions first, folding
the split into `input_feature` and appending a size-1 spatial dimension, which
turns the 2D convolution into a 3D spatial convolution that 2D spatial-minor
lowering can no longer match.

Because `SpaceToBatchConverter` runs before layout assignment and VMEM tiling,
skipping propagation (`disable_backprop_filter_propagation_max_batch_size`) has
to predict which convolutions downstream 2D spatial-minor lowering will accept
and run faster than space-to-batch (otherwise an unaccepted op falls back to an
unsplit spatial-major layout). Specifically, we assume `BF16` or `F32` types,
`batch` and `input_feature` smaller than one minor tile, a 2D filter area of at
most 64 so the `f32` accumulator fits in VMEM, and a spatial dimension large
enough (`window_size > batch`) for layout assignment to pick a supported
minor-tile layout and window dilation.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1024482094

display_title: Propagate comparison_order in elemental MLIR EmitCompare

head_commit.message:
Propagate comparison_order in elemental MLIR EmitCompare

`EmitCompare` in `xla/codegen/emitters/elemental_hlo_to_mlir.cc` previously set
`comparison_direction` on `mhlo::CompareOp` without populating `compare_type`.
As a result, `mapMhloOpToStdScalarOp<mhlo::CompareOp>` treated unexpanded
floating-point `WEAK` comparisons (such as CPU `WEAK` sort comparators skipped
by `ComparisonExpander`) and `TOTAL` comparisons as `PARTIAL` `arith.cmpf`
operations.

Populate `properties.compare_type` for floating-point comparisons from
`instr->comparison_order()` so signed-zero `WEAK` and `TOTAL` comparisons lower
to their corresponding `WEAKORDER` and `TOTALORDER` scalar expansions. Return
`UnimplementedError` for unsigned-zero `TOTAL` floating-point comparisons (which
require `ComparisonExpander`) and for unsupported non-partial complex
comparisons.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Add CuDnnGemmDimensions to compute the dimensions of cuDNN GEMM fusions with ShapeTracker.

`CuDnnFusionCompiler` derives the sizes and strides of the tensors of dot /
scaled-dot cuDNN fusions with `TritonFusionAnalysis`, which is part of the
legacy Triton GEMM tiling infrastructure that we want to remove: it no longer
tiles or emits fusions and does not support many of today's fusions.

`CuDnnGemmDimensions` replaces it in a follow-up change (cl/1018233906), using these steps:

1.  Use ShapeTracker to relate every instruction to one 'port' of the dot (lhs, rhs, output).
2.  Check cuDNN restrictions (i.e. non-scalar instructions must relate to the dot in a single way, because the cuDNN graph has a single tensor per instruction - for example, `dot(p, p)` and `d + transpose(d)` are rejected).
3.  Use ShapeTracker to record sizes and strides of each operand and output. This translates all bitcasts/transposes that are allowed into sizes and strides for cuDNN to read the correct tensor for operand (e.g. [batch, M, K] for lhs).

I haven't replaced TritonFusionAnalysis immediately because I still need to support strides and split-M, which happen in follow up CLs.

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Use the non-legacy Triton support check in `DotStrengthReduction`.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Use the non-legacy Triton support check in `DotStrengthReduction`.

`DotStrengthReduction` decides whether to strength-reduce a dot partly based on whether GemmFusion can handle it. It used `legacy_triton::CanTritonHandleGEMM` for this, but GemmFusion now uses `IsTritonSupportedInstruction` from `support.h`.

`IsTritonSupportedInstruction` only checks the instruction and assumes Triton is available on the target GPU. GemmFusion only runs on GPUs supported by Triton (CUDA Ampere+ and ROCm), so `DotStrengthReduction` now strength-reduces candidate dots on other GPUs (e.g. OneAPI, pre-Ampere CUDA), as reported by `EnsureTritonSupportsComputeCapability`. This also preserves the previous OneAPI behavior, where `CanTritonHandleGEMM` rejected all dots.

This is part of the effort to remove `support_legacy.cc`.

display_title: [XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

Region live range analysis repeatedly queried
`HloOrdering::GetExecutionConstraint` and linearly scanned accumulated control
edges on unordered instruction pairs, causing cubic blowups on high fanout
operands inside conditional branches. It also copied per computation instruction
maps on membership checks and scanned all region pairs after interference was
decided.

Answer same computation ordering queries directly from `HloReachabilityMap`
combined with transitive ancestor bitvectors over tentative control edges, and
cache directed cross computation queries. Store `LiveRangeRegions` as sorted
flat vectors, test smaller computation pairs first, stop scanning once
interference is forced, and add a same computation fast path in
`CallGraph::NearestAncestorsInSameComputation`. Move region analysis internals
into `copy_removal.cc`, replace `Relation` with a three bit ordering mask,
replace the per copy analysis budget in `CopyRemover::TryElideCopy` with
`ElideOptions`, store value nodes in a deque, and unify head and tail merge
checks.

Tests:
- `//xla/service:copy_insertion_test`: covers copy elision with many unordered
  readers, high fanout constant conditionals, transitive control edge cycle
  prevention, and interfering reads.

display_title: PR #52240: [XLA:GPU] Preserve frontend attributes in dot rewriters

head_commit.message:
PR #52240: [XLA:GPU] Preserve frontend attributes in dot rewriters

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52240

:pencil: **Summary of Changes**

Preserve frontend attributes when dot rewriters replace a dot with new instructions. New dots are added with `HloInstruction::AddInstruction` on the original dot, which derives them via `SetupDerivedInstruction` (also carrying metadata and, where shapes allow, sharding, like existing rewriters such as `DotDimensionSorter`), so they inherit the original dot's frontend attributes instead of silently dropping them. This covers `DotAlgorithmRewriter` (the BF16/TF32 decompositions in `backends/gpu/transforms` and the FP8xN decomposition in `hlo/transforms/dot_algorithm_rewriter.cc`), `ScaledDotRewriter`, `SplitkRewriter`, and `GemmFusionSwapOperands`.

:dart: **Justification**

Frontend attributes are the mechanism by which the frontend (e.g. JAX) attaches annotations to HLO instructions for downstream passes to consume. When a pass replaces an instruction, it must carry those attributes over to the replacement; otherwise the annotation is silently dropped and the consumers that depend on it no longer see it. These dot rewriters were not doing this, so annotated matmuls lost their scheduling annotations.

:compass: **Design: deriving replacements from the original dot**

Each new dot is added with `original_dot->AddInstruction(...)`, which derives it via `SetupDerivedInstruction` (metadata, frontend attributes, and sharding where the shapes allow). Instructions built by helpers call `SetupDerivedInstruction` directly: the instruction that replaces the dot in `RewriteDotWithOperandPairs` (shared by BF16X3/X6/X9 and TF32X3) and `RewriteFp8xNDot` (FP8X3/X4), and the split-K dot, which `MakeDotHlo` creates. So every new dot and the instruction that replaces the original keep the annotation.

:rocket: **Kind of Contribution**

:bug: Bug Fix

:test_tube: **Unit Tests:**

Added hardware-independent tests asserting frontend attributes survive each dot rewrite:

* `backends/gpu/transforms/dot_algorithm_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `KeepsFrontendAttributes`, parameterized over every `PrecisionConfig::Algorithm`: verifies that after the pass every dot and the instruction that replaces the dot keep the attributes. Without the fix it fails for the seven algorithms the pass decomposes (BF16, BF16X3/X6/X9, TF32X3, FP8X3/X4); new algorithms are covered automatically.
* `hlo/transforms/dot_algorithm_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `RewriteFp8xNDotStructureTest.KeepsFrontendAttributes`, for FP8X3 and FP8X4 at both precisions: verifies every F8 dot and the instruction that replaces the dot keep them.
* `gemm_fusion_swap_operands_test.cc`:
  * `SwappedDotKeepsFrontendAttributes`: verifies the swapped dot keeps them.
* `scaled_dot_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `RewrittenDotKeepsFrontendAttributes`: verifies the dot replacing a scaled-dot keeps them.
* `splitk_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `SplitKDotKeepsFrontendAttributes`: verifies the split-K dot keeps them.

:test_tube: **Execution Tests:**

No new checked-in execution test was added.

display_title: Fix spatial-minor backward weight conv rewrite on v6e+

head_commit.message:
Fix spatial-minor backward weight conv rewrite on v6e+

Small-batch and small-input-feature 2D backward-weight (`window_dilation`)
convolutions waste most of each 2D tile under spatial-major layouts and require
expensive layout-conversion copies, whereas spatial-minor lowering places a
large spatial dimension in the minor tile dimension directly. Right now,
`SpaceToBatchConverter` propagates splits into these convolutions first, folding
the split into `input_feature` and appending a size-1 spatial dimension, which
turns the 2D convolution into a 3D spatial convolution that 2D spatial-minor
lowering can no longer match.

Because `SpaceToBatchConverter` runs before layout assignment and VMEM tiling,
skipping propagation (`disable_backprop_filter_propagation_max_batch_size`) has
to predict which convolutions downstream 2D spatial-minor lowering will accept
and run faster than space-to-batch (otherwise an unaccepted op falls back to an
unsplit spatial-major layout). Specifically, we assume `BF16` or `F32` types,
`batch` and `input_feature` smaller than one minor tile, a 2D filter area of at
most 64 so the `f32` accumulator fits in VMEM, and a spatial dimension large
enough (`window_size > batch`) for layout assignment to pick a supported
minor-tile layout and window dilation.

display_title: [XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

Region live range analysis repeatedly queried
`HloOrdering::GetExecutionConstraint` and linearly scanned accumulated control
edges on unordered instruction pairs, causing cubic blowups on high fanout
operands inside conditional branches. It also copied per computation instruction
maps on membership checks and scanned all region pairs after interference was
decided.

Answer same computation ordering queries directly from `HloReachabilityMap`
combined with transitive ancestor bitvectors over tentative control edges, and
cache directed cross computation queries. Store `LiveRangeRegions` as sorted
flat vectors, test smaller computation pairs first, stop scanning once
interference is forced, and add a same computation fast path in
`CallGraph::NearestAncestorsInSameComputation`. Move region analysis internals
into `copy_removal.cc`, replace `Relation` with a three bit ordering mask,
replace the per copy analysis budget in `CopyRemover::TryElideCopy` with
`ElideOptions`, store value nodes in a deque, and unify head and tail merge
checks.

Tests:
- `//xla/service:copy_insertion_test`: covers copy elision with many unordered
  readers, high fanout constant conditionals, transitive control edge cycle
  prevention, and interfering reads.

display_title: Propagate comparison_order in elemental MLIR EmitCompare

head_commit.message:
Propagate comparison_order in elemental MLIR EmitCompare

`EmitCompare` in `xla/codegen/emitters/elemental_hlo_to_mlir.cc` previously set
`comparison_direction` on `mhlo::CompareOp` without populating `compare_type`.
As a result, `mapMhloOpToStdScalarOp<mhlo::CompareOp>` treated unexpanded
floating-point `WEAK` comparisons (such as CPU `WEAK` sort comparators skipped
by `ComparisonExpander`) and `TOTAL` comparisons as `PARTIAL` `arith.cmpf`
operations.

Populate `properties.compare_type` for floating-point comparisons from
`instr->comparison_order()` so signed-zero `WEAK` and `TOTAL` comparisons lower
to their corresponding `WEAKORDER` and `TOTALORDER` scalar expansions. Return
`UnimplementedError` for unsigned-zero `TOTAL` floating-point comparisons (which
require `ComparisonExpander`) and for unsupported non-partial complex
comparisons.

head_commit.message:
PR #52451: [XLA:GPU] Fix NULL child communicator after nonblocking NCCL split

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52451

📝 Summary of Changes

With nonblocking NCCL communicators, `ncclCommSplit` returns before the child communicator exists. XLA used the NULL child handle right away, and NCCL could later write to a variable that no longer existed.

This adds `NcclCommunicator::Split()`, which waits on the parent until the split finishes and only then returns the child. If a split fails with an uncertain outcome, the parent keeps the child-handle storage alive until it is torn down. `PollUntilDone` now reports a failed `ncclCommGetAsyncError` query separately from an async operation error.

🎯 Justification

Recoverable JAX jobs that use nonblocking communicators and communicator splitting can fail, and later crash, when XLA uses an uninitialized child.

🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix, 🧪 Tests

📊 Benchmark (for Performance Improvements)

N/A.

🧪 Unit Tests:

  Added regression tests:

- GpuCollectivesTest.SplitCommunicatorsNonblocking: a nonblocking split returns valid, healthy communicators.
- NcclErrorsTest.ReportsQueryFailureWithUnderlyingError and NcclErrorsTest.DistinguishesAsyncOperationErrorFromQueryFailure: query failures and async errors are reported differently.
- NcclTypesTest.AbortPendingSplits: null-handle handling, cleanup, and retention after an abort failure, using a fake abort (no GPU needed).

🧪 Execution Tests:

[XLA:GPU] Fix NULL child communicator after nonblocking NCCL split

With nonblocking NCCL communicators, ncclCommSplit can return before the
child handle is published. XLA read the output immediately, so it could
see a NULL child, and NCCL could later write to a stack variable that no
longer existed.

Add NcclCommunicator::Split(), which keeps the output on the heap and
polls the parent with ncclCommGetAsyncError until the split completes
before returning the child. If the wait fails or the child is
unexpectedly NULL, the output storage is leaked with a warning, since
NCCL may still write to it. Reclaiming it after parent teardown is left
for a follow-up.

display_title: PR #52240: [XLA:GPU] Preserve frontend attributes in dot rewriters

head_commit.message:
PR #52240: [XLA:GPU] Preserve frontend attributes in dot rewriters

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52240

:pencil: **Summary of Changes**

Preserve frontend attributes when dot rewriters replace a dot with new instructions. New dots are added with `HloInstruction::AddInstruction` on the original dot, which derives them via `SetupDerivedInstruction` (also carrying metadata and, where shapes allow, sharding, like existing rewriters such as `DotDimensionSorter`), so they inherit the original dot's frontend attributes instead of silently dropping them. This covers `DotAlgorithmRewriter` (the BF16/TF32 decompositions in `backends/gpu/transforms` and the FP8xN decomposition in `hlo/transforms/dot_algorithm_rewriter.cc`), `ScaledDotRewriter`, `SplitkRewriter`, and `GemmFusionSwapOperands`.

:dart: **Justification**

Frontend attributes are the mechanism by which the frontend (e.g. JAX) attaches annotations to HLO instructions for downstream passes to consume. When a pass replaces an instruction, it must carry those attributes over to the replacement; otherwise the annotation is silently dropped and the consumers that depend on it no longer see it. These dot rewriters were not doing this, so annotated matmuls lost their scheduling annotations.

:compass: **Design: deriving replacements from the original dot**

Each new dot is added with `original_dot->AddInstruction(...)`, which derives it via `SetupDerivedInstruction` (metadata, frontend attributes, and sharding where the shapes allow). Instructions built by helpers call `SetupDerivedInstruction` directly: the instruction that replaces the dot in `RewriteDotWithOperandPairs` (shared by BF16X3/X6/X9 and TF32X3) and `RewriteFp8xNDot` (FP8X3/X4), and the split-K dot, which `MakeDotHlo` creates. So every new dot and the instruction that replaces the original keep the annotation.

:rocket: **Kind of Contribution**

:bug: Bug Fix

:test_tube: **Unit Tests:**

Added hardware-independent tests asserting frontend attributes survive each dot rewrite:

* `backends/gpu/transforms/dot_algorithm_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `KeepsFrontendAttributes`, parameterized over every `PrecisionConfig::Algorithm`: verifies that after the pass every dot and the instruction that replaces the dot keep the attributes. Without the fix it fails for the seven algorithms the pass decomposes (BF16, BF16X3/X6/X9, TF32X3, FP8X3/X4); new algorithms are covered automatically.
* `hlo/transforms/dot_algorithm_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `RewriteFp8xNDotStructureTest.KeepsFrontendAttributes`, for FP8X3 and FP8X4 at both precisions: verifies every F8 dot and the instruction that replaces the dot keep them.
* `gemm_fusion_swap_operands_test.cc`:
  * `SwappedDotKeepsFrontendAttributes`: verifies the swapped dot keeps them.
* `scaled_dot_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `RewrittenDotKeepsFrontendAttributes`: verifies the dot replacing a scaled-dot keeps them.
* `splitk_rewriter_test.cc`:
  * `SplitKDotKeepsFrontendAttributes`: verifies the split-K dot keeps them.

:test_tube: **Execution Tests:**

No new checked-in execution test was added.

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

Previously, `--xla_gpu_execution_progress_tracking` only wired its progress dump to the host-side terminate watchdog (`--xla_gpu_execution_terminate_timeout`). When a kernel or collective hung on the device after host dispatch returned (`--xla_gpu_device_execution_terminate_timeout` or `ExecutionTimeoutHandler`), the process aborted without logging completed or pending thunks.

So this change extracts `LogExecutionProgress` (logging `[<device_ordinal>]` context on every line, nested `kCommandBuffer` thunks for pending command buffers, and `Last pending thunks` only when `num_pending > max_thunks_to_log`) and wires it to `HangWatchdog::Abort` for both host and device terminate timeouts as well as `ExecutionTimeoutGuards` via `std::shared_ptr<ProgressTracker>` captured in the watchdog callbacks (which `device_guards` keeps alive in `main_stream->DoHostCallback` until enqueued device work completes).

head_commit.message:
PR #52609: [ROCm] Port StreamExecutor test cases and fix the gaps they expose

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/52609

📝 Summary of Changes
- RocmExecutor::IsHostMemoryPinned left start_addr/range_size
  uninitialized when hipDrvPointerGetAttributes does not populate them,
  so the containment check read indeterminate stack values.

- RocmExecutor::GetPointerMemorySpace returned InternalError for
  hipMallocManaged memory. It now queries HIP_POINTER_ATTRIBUTE_IS_MANAGED
  first and maps managed/unified memory types to MemorySpace::kUnified

- RocmStream only declared the single-argument DoHostCallbackWithStatus,
  which name-hid the error_cb overload and silently dropped asynchronous
  callback failures. The overload is now implemented, including invoking
  error_cb when the callback cannot be enqueued.

Test cases added:
  - rocm_kernel_test:   ArityZeroKernelSkipsArgumentCountCheck
  - rocm_executor_test: IsHostMemoryPinnedWorksWithRegisteredHostMemory
                      GetPointerMemorySpaceWorksWithUnifiedMemory
  - rocm_stream_test:   DoHostCallbackWithStatusSuccess
                      DoHostCallbackWithStatusError

🎯 Justification
Add more unit test coverage on ROCm platform

🚀 Kind of Contribution:🧪 Tests

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Dump progress on GPU device execution timeouts

Previously, `--xla_gpu_execution_progress_tracking` only wired its progress dump to the host-side terminate watchdog (`--xla_gpu_execution_terminate_timeout`). When a kernel or collective hung on the device after host dispatch returned (`--xla_gpu_device_execution_terminate_timeout` or `ExecutionTimeoutHandler`), the process aborted without logging completed or pending thunks.

So this change extracts `LogExecutionProgress` (logging `[<device_ordinal>]` context on every line, nested `kCommandBuffer` thunks for pending command buffers, and `Last pending thunks` only when `num_pending > max_thunks_to_log`) and wires it to `HangWatchdog::Abort` for both host and device terminate timeouts as well as `ExecutionTimeoutGuards` via `std::shared_ptr<ProgressTracker>` captured in the watchdog callbacks (which `device_guards` keeps alive in `main_stream->DoHostCallback` until enqueued device work completes).

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Use the non-legacy Triton support check in `DotStrengthReduction`.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Use the non-legacy Triton support check in `DotStrengthReduction`.

`DotStrengthReduction` decides whether to strength-reduce a dot partly based on whether GemmFusion can handle it. It used `legacy_triton::CanTritonHandleGEMM` for this, but GemmFusion now uses `IsTritonSupportedInstruction` from `support.h`.

`IsTritonSupportedInstruction` only checks the instruction and assumes Triton is available on the target GPU. GemmFusion only runs on GPUs supported by Triton (CUDA Ampere+ and ROCm), so `DotStrengthReduction` now strength-reduces candidate dots on other GPUs (e.g. OneAPI, pre-Ampere CUDA), as reported by `EnsureTritonSupportsComputeCapability`. This also preserves the previous OneAPI behavior, where `CanTritonHandleGEMM` rejected all dots.

This is part of the effort to remove `support_legacy.cc`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1023470801

display_title: Fix spatial-minor backward weight conv rewrite on v6e+

head_commit.message:
Fix spatial-minor backward weight conv rewrite on v6e+

Small-batch and small-input-feature 2D backward-weight (`window_dilation`)
convolutions waste most of each 2D tile under spatial-major layouts and require
expensive layout-conversion copies, whereas spatial-minor lowering places a
large spatial dimension in the minor tile dimension directly. Right now,
`SpaceToBatchConverter` propagates splits into these convolutions first, folding
the split into `input_feature` and appending a size-1 spatial dimension, which
turns the 2D convolution into a 3D spatial convolution that 2D spatial-minor
lowering can no longer match.

Because `SpaceToBatchConverter` runs before layout assignment and VMEM tiling,
skipping propagation (`disable_backprop_filter_propagation_max_batch_size`) has
to predict which convolutions downstream 2D spatial-minor lowering will accept
and run faster than space-to-batch (otherwise an unaccepted op falls back to an
unsplit spatial-major layout). Specifically, we assume `BF16` or `F32` types,
`batch` and `input_feature` smaller than one minor tile, a 2D filter area of at
most 64 so the `f32` accumulator fits in VMEM, and a spatial dimension large
enough (`window_size > batch`) for layout assignment to pick a supported
minor-tile layout and window dilation.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 1018243846

display_title: Propagate comparison_order in elemental MLIR EmitCompare

head_commit.message:
Propagate comparison_order in elemental MLIR EmitCompare

`EmitCompare` in `xla/codegen/emitters/elemental_hlo_to_mlir.cc` previously set
`comparison_direction` on `mhlo::CompareOp` without populating `compare_type`.
As a result, `mapMhloOpToStdScalarOp<mhlo::CompareOp>` treated unexpanded
floating-point `WEAK` comparisons (such as CPU `WEAK` sort comparators skipped
by `ComparisonExpander`) and `TOTAL` comparisons as `PARTIAL` `arith.cmpf`
operations.

Populate `properties.compare_type` for floating-point comparisons from
`instr->comparison_order()` so signed-zero `WEAK` and `TOTAL` comparisons lower
to their corresponding `WEAKORDER` and `TOTALORDER` scalar expansions. Return
`UnimplementedError` for unsigned-zero `TOTAL` floating-point comparisons (which
require `ComparisonExpander`) and for unsupported non-partial complex
comparisons.

display_title: [XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Simplify and speed up region analysis in copy removal

Region live range analysis repeatedly queried
`HloOrdering::GetExecutionConstraint` and linearly scanned accumulated control
edges on unordered instruction pairs, causing cubic blowups on high fanout
operands inside conditional branches. It also copied per computation instruction
maps on membership checks and scanned all region pairs after interference was
decided.

Answer same computation ordering queries directly from `HloReachabilityMap`
combined with transitive ancestor bitvectors over tentative control edges, and
cache directed cross computation queries. Store `LiveRangeRegions` as sorted
flat vectors, test smaller computation pairs first, stop scanning once
interference is forced, and add a same computation fast path in
`CallGraph::NearestAncestorsInSameComputation`. Move region analysis internals
into `copy_removal.cc`, replace `Relation` with a three bit ordering mask,
replace the per copy analysis budget in `CopyRemover::TryElideCopy` with

name: CI ROCm
display_title: [XLA:GPU] Let slice and dynamic-slice change layout

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Only let a slice of an array with a fixed layout change the layout

GpuLayoutAssignment let every slice and dynamic-slice produce its result in
a layout that differs from the layout of the sliced operand, so that a
layout required by a consumer does not reach the sliced operand. That is the
intent for a parameter or loop state: converting such an array converts all
of it, possibly outside of the loop that slices it.

For an array that is computed in the same computation it is harmful. The
layout required by the consumers of the slice stops at the slice, and the
sliced array takes whatever other preference reaches it. In the attention
of MaxText gpt-oss-20b the softmax input bf16[4,64,4096,4097] is sliced to
[4,64,4096,4096] for a dot, and is also reduced to a [4,64,4096] array that
is transposed. The preference of that small transposed result gave the
softmax input and everything it is computed from the layout {3,1,2,0}, and
the slice had to transpose the large array. The step time went up by 2.5%.

Let a slice or dynamic-slice change the layout only if the sliced array is a
parameter or an element of a parameter or while loop tuple. Every other
slice keeps the layout of its operand in both directions, as before slices
could change the layout. This also covers the constant, iota and broadcast
operands that were handled as a preference, so that special case is
removed.

GpuLayoutAssignment::InstructionCanChangeLayoutBeforeNormalization still
accepts every slice, because the passes that run before LayoutNormalization
may replace the operand of a layout-changing slice.

display_title: [IFRT] Validate non-negative dimensions and element-count bounds in `xla::ifrt::Shape`

head_commit.message:
[IFRT] Validate non-negative dimensions and element-count bounds in `xla::ifrt::Shape`

Constructing an `xla::ifrt::Shape` deferred negative-dimension checks to `Shape::num_elements()` and permitted dimensions whose total element count overflowed `int64_t` or exceeded what bit-size and byte-size calculations could represent. Callers computing `shape.num_elements() * dtype.bit_size()` or `shape.num_elements() * dtype.byte_size()` could silently wrap signed `int64_t` unless every backend and utility repeated its own checked multiplication.

Add `Shape::Create` to validate non-negative dimensions and that the product of non-zero dimensions fits within `Shape::kMaxNumElements` (`INT64_MAX / 128`, accommodating elements up to 128 bits), returning `absl::InvalidArgumentError` on invalid dimensions, and delegate `Shape`'s constructor (via `CHECK_OK`) and `Shape::FromProto` to `Shape::Create`. Enforce the same `Shape::kMaxNumElements` bound in `IfrtArrayType::verify`, `VifrtArrayV1Type::verify`, and `PjRtExecutable` shape conversions, remove `Shape::NumElements()`, drop redundant downstream negative-dimension and byte-size overflow checks, and update IFRT unit tests that constructed `Shape` with negative dimensions.

display_title: [XLA:PjRt] Raise TransposePlan memcpy threshold from 1 MiB to 64 MiB

head_commit.message:
[XLA:PjRt] Raise TransposePlan memcpy threshold from 1 MiB to 64 MiB

Unchunked `inner_kernel_is_memcpy()` plans in `xla/pjrt/transpose.cc` previously used a 1 MiB (`1 << 20`) per-thread parallelization threshold while non-memcpy transpose plans used 64 MiB (`1 << 26`). When memory-bandwidth-bound 1-D or tiled contiguous copies larger than 1 MiB run via `TransposePlan` alongside concurrent async transfers, fanning each copy out across up to 16 threads adds host CPU contention and thread overhead without reducing aggregate H2D wall time.

Unify `kMinBytesPerThread` for `chunk_contiguity_ == ChunkContiguity::kNone` to 64 MiB (`1 << 26`) regardless of `inner_kernel_is_memcpy()`, matching non-memcpy transpose plans and the 64 MiB `kFastPathMaxBytes` threshold in `xla/pjrt/tiled_linearizer.cc`. Plans with contiguous chunking (`ChunkContiguity::kOutput` / `ChunkContiguity::kInput`) keep `kMinBytesPerThread = 1` so chunked pipelined transfers remain parallelized below 64 MiB.

Testing:
* Added `TransposeTest.MemcpyParallelizationThreshold` in `xla/pjrt/transpose_test.cc` covering 16 MiB, 64 MiB, and 128 MiB 1-D copies (`kNone`) and 16 MiB 2-D tiled copies (`kNone` vs `kOutput`).
* Ran `//xla/pjrt:transpose_test` (all shards pass).
* In a 51-step A/B profile of concurrent async H2D transfers on a multi-host TPU training workload, this cut host thread-summed `Transpose::ExecuteChunk` time by 33% (224.9 → 150.0 ms/step), cut host thread count in the trace by 35% (642 → 416), and kept H2D wall-clock union span flat (13.38 → 13.27 ms/step).

name: CI ROCm
display_title: [PJRT] Replace TransposePlan::Node execution with a flat op array.

head_commit.message:
[PJRT] Replace TransposePlan::Node execution with a flat op array.

Before this change, `TransposePlan` ran transposes by walking a linked graph of
`Node` structs through several heavily templated recursive functions
(`Transpose`, `TransposeConstStride1`, `MacroKernel`, `StridedMemset`), with
separate code paths for padding fills, sub-byte packing, and EF57 conversion
(splitting each `double` into two `float`s, high and low). That made the
execution code hard to follow and hard to extend with new tiled or packed
layouts.

This CL replaces those drivers with a simpler two-step model in
`xla/pjrt/transpose.{h,cc}` and `xla/pjrt/transpose_kernels.{h,cc}`:

1. **Build a small tree of operations** describing what a chunk of work needs
   to do:
   - Control flow: `Seq` (run children in order), `Offset` (shift the `a`/`b`
     pointers), `Loop` (repeat a child with byte strides `da`/`db`), and
     `Pipe` (run step 1 into a scratch buffer, then step 2 out of it).
   - Work items (leaves): `Transpose2D`, `Copy1D` (`memcpy`), `Fill1D` (`memset`
     for padding), `PackSubbyte`, and `ConvertEf57`.
2. **Flatten that tree into one contiguous array** of 56-byte `TransposeOp`
   structs. Every op has the same function signature:

   ```cpp
   void fn(const TransposeOp* op, const char* a, char* b, char* scratch);
   ```

   Running a chunk is just `ops[0].fn(&ops[0], a, b, scratch);`. Children live
   immediately after their parent in the array (`op + 1` and `op + op->right_off`).
   For example, `Seq(A, B)` flattens to:

   ```text
   [0] Seq { right_off = 2 }  // calls [1], then tail-calls [2]
   [1] A
   [2] B
   ```

### Concrete examples of the tricky cases

**1. Splitting partial tiles ahead of time**
Previously, 2D transpose kernels handled uneven tile edges with runtime branches
inside templates. Now `BuildChunkPlan` splits any tile that isn't a multiple of
the SIMD block size into exact pieces. For example, transposing a 10x10 `float`
matrix (`4` bytes/elem, row stride `40` bytes) with an 8x8 SIMD block becomes:

```text
Seq(
  Transpose2D(a_elems=8, b_elems=8),    // rows 0..7, cols 0..7 (SIMD)
  Offset(da=320, db=32,
    Transpose2D(a_elems=8, b_elems=2)), // bottom 2 rows, cols 0..7 (scalar)
  Offset(da=32, db=320,
    Transpose2D(a_elems=2, b_elems=10)) // right 2 cols, all 10 rows (scalar)
)
```

Every leaf op now handles one uniform shape with no edge-case branching.

**2. Fusing the innermost loop into ops**
Wrapping a leaf in a separate `Loop`—for example `Loop(count=128, Transpose2D)`—would
make 128 indirect calls and enter/exit the AVX kernel 128 times. Instead,
`FlattenPlan` folds the trip count directly into the leaf:

```text
// Before:
Loop(count=128, da=..., db=..., Transpose2D(...))

// After (1 entry = 56 bytes, 1 call instead of 128 indirect calls):
Transpose2D(count=128, da=..., db=...)
```

It does the same for every leaf op and for `Pipe`.

**3. Fusing 2D copies with a short trailing chunk (`Copy2D`)**
Tiled layouts often copy rows made of a few full chunks plus a shorter tail.
For example, copying 4 rows of 289 bytes out of tiled memory (two 128-byte
chunks spaced 512 bytes apart, plus a 33-byte tail at offset `2*512 = 1024`):

```text
// Before (without Copy2D: 5 entries, 4 indirect calls per row):
Loop(count=4, da=128, db=289,
  Seq(
    Loop(count=2, da=512, db=128, Copy1D(bytes=128)),
    Offset(da=1024, db=256, Copy1D(bytes=33))))

// After (2 entries = 112 bytes, 1 call total):
Copy2D(count=4, da=128, db=289,
       inner_count=2, inner_da=512, inner_db=128,
       bytes=128, tail_bytes=33)
```

(`Copy2D` is introduced during flattening and uses 2 adjacent `TransposeOp`
slots—storing the inner-loop fields in `op + 1`—so `TransposeOp` stays 56
bytes.) It executes a plain nested loop (never forming past-the-end pointers
when strides are negative):

```cpp
for (int64_t i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
  const char* row_a = a + i * 128;
  char* row_b = b + i * 289;
  for (int64_t j = 0; j < 2; ++j) {
    std::memcpy(row_b + j * 128, row_a + j * 512, 128);
  }
  std::memcpy(row_b + 2 * 128, row_a + 2 * 512, 33);
}
```

**4. Temporary scratch buffers & EF57 (`Pipe` + `ConvertEf57`)**
Padding fills, sub-byte packing, and `float64 -> EF57` conversion now live in
the same plan tree. For example, converting and transposing 120 rows of 16
strided `double`s into EF57 looks like:

```text
// Plan tree:
Loop(count=120, ...,
  Pipe(bytes=128,
    Loop(count=16, ..., ConvertEf57(doubles=1)), // 16 doubles -> 128-byte scratch of (hi, lo) float pairs
    Transpose2D(a_elems=2, b_elems=16)))         // transpose so the 16 hi floats and 16 lo floats sit together

// Lowered (both loops fused into their ops):
Pipe(count=120, bytes=128, ...,
  ConvertEf57(count=16, doubles=1, ...),
  Transpose2D(count=1, a_elems=2, b_elems=16, ...))
```

Plans that need no scratch pass `nullptr`. When scratch is needed, buffers up
to 4 KiB live on the stack (larger ones use a 64-byte-aligned heap allocation).
For `doubles == 1`, `ConvertEf57` calls `SplitF64ToF32` inline instead of
making a cross-file call to `ConvertF64ToEf57` for one element at a time.

**5. Stopping the compiler from running out of registers in `OpFullTranspose2DHwy`**
For an 8x8 tile, the inner kernel loads 8 rows (`a`, `a + lda`, ...,
`a + 7*lda`). Once we fused the outer `k` loop around the inlined tile kernel,
LLVM tried to turn all 8 row addresses into 8 separate running pointers across
`k`. On x86-64 (15 integer registers), that ran out of registers and spilled
loop counters to the stack. A small inline-asm barrier macro
(`XLA_HIDE_POINTER_FROM_OPTIMIZER`: `asm("" : "+r"(ptr))` on GCC/Clang, zero
instructions and no `"memory"` clobber) hides the stepped pointers from LLVM
so it goes back to computing row addresses from one base pointer with no stack
spills.

**6. Picking SIMD kernels once at plan creation**
`GetTransposeMacroKernelOp` and `GetPackSubbyteOp` pick the right Highway SIMD
function when building the plan rather than per tile. Because plans are cached,
we eagerly initialize Highway's global target cache first
(`hwy::GetChosenTarget().Update(...)`); without that, the first plan built in a
process caches Highway's lazy-init stub (`ChooseAndCall`) and re-runs CPUID on
every call forever. Also removes the unused `bs = 1` kernel instantiation.

### Tests (`xla/pjrt/transpose_test.cc`)
- Added 64-byte guard bytes before and after test output buffers to catch
  out-of-bounds writes.
- Added unit tests for multi-threaded partial-tile padding, eager Highway target
  initialization (`InitializesHighwayTargetEagerly`), `OpCopy2D` fusion edge
  cases including negative strides and partial tiles (`OpCopy2DFusionEdgeCases`),
  and strided single-double EF57 special IEEE values (`±0`, `±Inf`, `NaN`,
  subnormals) (`F64ToEf57StridedDoubles1SpecialValues`).

### Benchmarks (`BM_Transpose*`, cpu/op, AVX2 / Haswell, 1 core, 10 runs, 0.05s/run)

```text
name                                                      base           new            vs base
BM_Transpose_uint8_threads_1_256_256_perm_1_0              3.179µ ±  1%   3.150µ ±  8%        ~ (p=0.143 n=10)
BM_Transpose_float_threads_1_256_256_perm_1_0              8.428µ ±  8%   7.763µ ±  7%   -7.89% (p=0.019 n=10)
```

display_title: [XLA:PjRt] Raise TransposePlan memcpy threshold from 1 MiB to 64 MiB

head_commit.message:
[XLA:PjRt] Raise TransposePlan memcpy threshold from 1 MiB to 64 MiB

Unchunked `inner_kernel_is_memcpy()` plans in `xla/pjrt/transpose.cc` previously used a 1 MiB (`1 << 20`) per-thread parallelization threshold while non-memcpy transpose plans used 64 MiB (`1 << 26`). When memory-bandwidth-bound 1-D or tiled contiguous copies larger than 1 MiB run via `TransposePlan` alongside concurrent async transfers, fanning each copy out across up to 16 threads adds host CPU contention and thread overhead without reducing aggregate H2D wall time.

Unify `kMinBytesPerThread` for `chunk_contiguity_ == ChunkContiguity::kNone` to 64 MiB (`1 << 26`) regardless of `inner_kernel_is_memcpy()`, matching non-memcpy transpose plans and the 64 MiB `kFastPathMaxBytes` threshold in `xla/pjrt/tiled_linearizer.cc`. Plans with contiguous chunking (`ChunkContiguity::kOutput` / `ChunkContiguity::kInput`) keep `kMinBytesPerThread = 1` so chunked pipelined transfers remain parallelized below 64 MiB.

Testing:
* Added `TransposeTest.MemcpyParallelizationThreshold` in `xla/pjrt/transpose_test.cc` covering 16 MiB, 64 MiB, and 128 MiB 1-D copies (`kNone`) and 16 MiB 2-D tiled copies (`kNone` vs `kOutput`).
* Ran `//xla/pjrt:transpose_test` (all shards pass).
* In a 51-step A/B profile of concurrent async H2D transfers on a multi-host TPU training workload, this cut host thread-summed `Transpose::ExecuteChunk` time by 33% (224.9 → 150.0 ms/step), cut host thread count in the trace by 35% (642 → 416), and kept H2D wall-clock union span flat (13.38 → 13.27 ms/step).

display_title: [XLA:GPU] Fuse second-stage tree reductions into Triton norm consumers.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Fuse second-stage tree reductions into Triton norm consumers.

***Problem:*** Wide normalizations split by `TreeReductionRewriter` leave their tiny second-stage reduction and elementwise epilogue as separate launch-bound kernels, because `SoftmaxRewriterTriton` only runs before the split and its profitability check ignores kernel launch overhead.

***Solution:*** Run `SoftmaxRewriterTriton` again after `TreeReductionRewriter` so it fuses the second-stage reduction into the normalization consumer while the first stage stays a separate high-occupancy kernel, and charge the unfused alternative one kernel launch overhead per extra kernel.

head_commit.message:
[XLA:GPU] Fuse launch-bound disjoint-slice reduction siblings.

***Problem:*** `GpuMultiOutputFusion` rejects sibling reductions that read non-overlapping slices of a shared parameter, so tiny slice reductions such as the K and V parts of a decode-step QKV reduction each pay a separate kernel launch.

***Solution:*** Allow same-shape sibling reductions over disjoint slices of a shared parameter to fuse when the GPU performance model estimates both below the kernel launch overhead, where the saved launch outweighs either kernel's runtime.

Donate PjRt-IFRT executable inputs according to donation intent.

`LoadedExecutable::GetDonatableInputIndices()` reports parameter donation intent (`jax.buffer_donor` and `tf.aliasing_output`), whereas XLA compilation may leave a donor unaliased when no compatible output buffer exists. name: CI ROCm
display_title: Add post-scheduling control dependencies to async callers in CopyRemover.

head_commit.message:
Add post-scheduling control dependencies to async callers in CopyRemover.

**Problem:**
When post-scheduling `CopyRemover` deletes a copy so that an old value (`src`) and a new value (`dst`) share the same physical buffer, it must add a control dependency from every reader of `src` to the instruction that writes `dst`. This prevents later passes (such as `HloRematerialization`) from moving or cloning a read of `src` past the point where `dst` overwrites the shared buffer.

For asynchronous operations (such as `dynamic-slice-start`), the output value `dst` is defined by the inner instruction inside the child `async_wrapped_computation`, not in the parent computation. Previously:
1. When checking *whether* the copy could be deleted, `LiveRangeBefore` resolved the inner async instruction to its `kAsyncStart` caller in the parent computation and approved sharing the buffer.
2. However, when adding the control dependency *after* deleting the copy, `add_control_deps` saw that the reader of `src` (in the parent computation) and the inner async instruction (in the child computation) had different `parent()` computations, and silently skipped adding the control edge.

Without that control dependency, `HloRematerialization` could clone a reader of `src` to a point in the schedule after `kAsyncStart`, causing it to read the shared buffer while the background async DMA was overwriting it.

**Fix:**
1. In `add_control_deps`, resolve instructions inside an async computation to their `kAsyncStart` caller so the control dependency (`reader_of_src -> kAsyncStart`) is added in the parent computation.
2. Check `ordering_->ExecutesBefore(use_instr, dst_instr)` before adding the edge so that in-place async operations (where `src->uses` also includes `kAsyncDone` / `kAsyncUpdate`, which executes *after* `kAsyncStart`) do not add a backward control edge from `kAsyncDone` back to `kAsyncStart`.

display_title: [IFRT IR] Adopt `CalleeSymbolManager` in `IfrtDcePass`

head_commit.message:
[IFRT IR] Adopt `CalleeSymbolManager` in `IfrtDcePass`

`IfrtDcePass` previously maintained its own symbol-use counts and cloning logic that missed several edge cases: single-use public callees had their signatures mutated in place, shared live callees with pure dead ops were cloned unnecessarily before simplifying, recursive outlined callees were mutated without isolating internal `func.call` references, and dead-callee erasure was sensitive to reverse-walk order with no tracking of erased transfer/remap ops or unreachable `func.call` references.

Replaces the ad-hoc `ResolveCallee` and cloning logic with `CalleeSymbolManager`. Simplifies distinct defined callees (including shared and public callees) in place via `mlir::simplifyRegions` upfront so dead symbol references inside unreachable blocks are dropped before the reverse walk checks exclusivity.

As part of adopting `CalleeSymbolManager::Create` and `GetCallee`, `ifrt.Call` ops targeting external declarations, undefined callees, or callees nested deeper than one `ModuleOp` now emit an op error and fail the pass instead of being silently skipped. The pass also fails on unregistered region-bearing ops in the root module or in a mutated outlined module.

name: CI ROCm
display_title: [IFRT IR] Introduce `CalleeSymbolManager` for copy-on-write callee management

head_commit.message:
[IFRT IR] Introduce `CalleeSymbolManager` for copy-on-write callee management

Mutating or erasing an `ifrt.Call` callee safely requires knowing whether its top-level root symbol (a flat `FuncOp` or an enclosing outlined `ModuleOp`) is public or referenced by other callers, while keeping symbol tables and root-scope use counts synchronized across cloning, redirection, in-place edits, and erasure. Repeating ad-hoc `SymbolTable::getSymbolUses` walks or custom cloning logic across individual passes risks quadratic symbol scans, stale symbol tables, and unnecessary full-module clones.

Adds `CalleeSymbolManager`, which provides the following capabilities:
* **Single-pass root-scope indexing (`Create`)**: Scans root-scope symbol uses once when constructed to support constant-time exclusivity checks. Emits an op error and fails if root-scope symbol uses cannot be determined (for example, due to an unregistered region-bearing op).
* **Callee resolution and validation (`GetCallee`)**: Resolves a defined `FuncOp` callee and emits an op error if the call is outside the root symbol scope, the callee is missing or external, or the callee is nested more than one `ModuleOp` deep.
* **Group-aware copy-on-write cloning (`GetOrCloneCalleeForMutation`)**: Mutates a private callee in place when a group of `ifrt.Call` ops accounts for all root-scope uses of its root symbol; otherwise clones a private copy and redirects every call in the group. For outlined callees with internal symbol references inside the enclosing `ModuleOp` (such as recursive calls), splits the unmutated copy into a private helper so internal callers remain isolated without forcing an extra module clone on sole-caller private modules. Fails with an op error before mutating IR if internal symbol uses cannot be determined.
* **Call redirection (`RedirectCallToCallee`)**: Redirects an `ifrt.Call` op to another callee in place while updating cached root-symbol use counts and tracking the detached original root symbol for later cleanup.
* **Scoped mutation tracking (`RecordOpCreated`, `RecordOpErased`, `RecordOpMutation`)**: Keeps cached root-scope use counts synchronized across external op insertions, erasures, and in-place mutations (automatically ignoring ops inside nested `SymbolTable`s).
* **Transitive dead-symbol erasure and deferred sweeps (`EraseCallAndMaybeEraseCallee`, `EraseUnusedTrackedRootSymbols`)**: Erases an `ifrt.Call` and transitively removes any now-unused private non-IFRT root symbols (preserving public symbols and `ifrt.function` / `ifrt.reshard_function` entry points), invalidating nested symbol tables before erasure. Tracks detached root symbols whose remaining references drop later so an end-of-pass sweep can clean them up regardless of traversal order.

head_commit.message:
[IFRT IR] Adopt `CalleeSymbolManager` in `IfrtCallDedupPass`

`IfrtCallDedupPass` maintained ad-hoc root-symbol counting, copy-on-write cloning, and `BumpPtrAllocator`-backed variant caching. When a private outlined module had internal `func.call` references, it cloned the entire module even for a sole caller, and when every call to a shared private callee was redirected to a cached specialized clone, the original symbol was left behind as dead IR.

Replaces the custom symbol-use tracking and cloning helpers with `CalleeSymbolManager`, migrates the specialized-callee cache from `llvm::DenseMap` + `llvm::BumpPtrAllocator` to `absl::flat_hash_map` with `absl::InlinedVector` keys, and erases newly unused private non-IFRT original root symbols via `EraseUnusedTrackedRootSymbols()` at pass exit. Sole-caller private outlined modules with internal references now split the unmutated callee into a private helper in place without cloning the enclosing module, and the pass fails cleanly on unregistered region-bearing ops in the root module. External declarations and multi-block callees continue to be skipped during upfront collection.

display_title: [XLA] Always use region analysis in copy removal

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Always use region analysis in copy removal

After speeding up region live range analysis in `CopyRemover`, the non region
fallback only leaves avoidable copies behind when unordered readers and in place
updates can be ordered by control dependencies.

Remove `use_region_based_live_range_analysis` from `CopyInsertion` and
`CopyRemover`, always fall back to region interference analysis when whole value
ordering is inconclusive, and deprecate the CPU and GPU
`xla_{cpu,gpu}_copy_insertion_use_region_analysis` flags as no ops. Delete the
now redundant `OrderPredecessorReadersBeforeInPlaceCopies` prepass, since region
analysis handles chained in place updates directly without adding control edges
to retained copies. Treat distinct values defined by the same multi output
instruction as interfering so separate in place outputs never share one buffer,
and preserve control dependencies on hoisted while loop calls in
`SmallWhileLoopHoistingPass`.

Tests:

name: CI ROCm
display_title: [IFRT IR] Introduce `CalleeSymbolManager` for copy-on-write callee management

head_commit.message:
[IFRT IR] Introduce `CalleeSymbolManager` for copy-on-write callee management

Mutating or erasing an `ifrt.Call` callee safely requires knowing whether its top-level root symbol (a flat `FuncOp` or an enclosing outlined `ModuleOp`) is public or referenced by other callers, while keeping symbol tables and root-scope use counts synchronized across cloning, redirection, in-place edits, and erasure. Repeating ad-hoc `SymbolTable::getSymbolUses` walks or custom cloning logic across individual passes risks quadratic symbol scans, stale symbol tables, and unnecessary full-module clones.

Adds `CalleeSymbolManager`, which provides the following capabilities:
* **Single-pass root-scope indexing (`Create`)**: Scans root-scope symbol uses once when constructed to support constant-time exclusivity checks. Emits an op error and fails if root-scope symbol uses cannot be determined (for example, due to an unregistered region-bearing op).
* **Callee resolution and validation (`GetCallee`)**: Resolves a defined `FuncOp` callee and emits an op error if the call is outside the root symbol scope, the callee is missing or external, or the callee is nested more than one `ModuleOp` deep.
* **Group-aware copy-on-write cloning (`GetOrCloneCalleeForMutation`)**: Mutates a private callee in place when a group of `ifrt.Call` ops accounts for all root-scope uses of its root symbol; otherwise clones a private copy and redirects every call in the group. For outlined callees with internal symbol references inside the enclosing `ModuleOp` (such as recursive calls), splits the unmutated copy into a private helper so internal callers remain isolated without forcing an extra module clone on sole-caller private modules. Fails with an op error before mutating IR if internal symbol uses cannot be determined.
* **Call redirection (`RedirectCallToCallee`)**: Redirects an `ifrt.Call` op to another callee in place while updating cached root-symbol use counts and tracking the detached original root symbol for later cleanup.
* **Scoped mutation tracking (`RecordOpCreated`, `RecordOpErased`, `RecordOpMutation`)**: Keeps cached root-scope use counts synchronized across external op insertions, erasures, and in-place mutations (automatically ignoring ops inside nested `SymbolTable`s).
* **Transitive dead-symbol erasure and deferred sweeps (`EraseCallAndMaybeEraseCallee`, `EraseUnusedTrackedRootSymbols`)**: Erases an `ifrt.Call` and transitively removes any now-unused private non-IFRT root symbols (preserving public symbols and `ifrt.function` / `ifrt.reshard_function` entry points), invalidating nested symbol tables before erasure. Tracks detached root symbols whose remaining references drop later so an end-of-pass sweep can clean them up regardless of traversal order.

head_commit.message:
[XLA] Return std::nullopt from PatternMatchParseWhileLoop for infinite and constant-condition loops

`PatternMatchParseWhileLoop` previously returned `ParsedStaticWhileLoop` with `-1` sentinels (`trip_count = -1` in `HandleNoopLoopCondition` for infinite boolean-flag loops, and `induction_var_index = -1` with `trip_count = -1` or `0` in `HandleStaticLoopComparison` for constant comparisons). Callers such as `TryParseAndEvaluateWhileInductionVar` and `WhileLoopAnalysis::ComputeLoopStatistics` only checked `is_dynamic()` before indexing `while_hlo->shape().tuple_shapes(-1)`, triggering an out-of-bounds read and AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free (#49823).

Return `std::nullopt` from `PatternMatchParseWhileLoop` for infinite boolean-flag loops and constant-comparison conditions (and bounds-check `tuple_index` in `EvaluateWhileLoopParamInitValue`), `CHECK` the non-negative `trip_count` and valid `induction_var_index` invariants in `HloEvaluator`, and compute `induction_var_init_value + trip_count * step_size` in `uint64_t` in `TryParseAndEvaluateWhileInductionVar` to avoid signed integer overflow matching `HandleWhile`.
